title: Unguided Machine Learning-Based Computation Offloading for Near-Memory Processing
problem: Data-intensive applications face memory wall bottlenecks in traditional processor-centric architectures. Supervised ML-based offloading requires extensive labeled datasets. Naive application-wide offloading to near-memory processing (NMP) cores underutilizes due to lower processing power.
motivation: 3D-enabled NMP architectures can eliminate off-chip data transfer bottlenecks. However, existing supervised ML approaches are labor-intensive to deploy and fail to optimize partial offloading decisions.
method: The approach watches an application run and automatically divides its code into two groups: the parts the CPU handles efficiently and the parts that would run faster on near-memory processors (specialized cores positioned closer to where data is stored). Unlike previous methods that need a large set of labeled examples to learn from, this approach figures out these groups on its own. It then offloads only the memory-intensive portions—the parts where the application spends most time waiting for data—so the overall performance improves without wasting computing power on unnecessary offloading.
key_novelty: This is the first approach to use unsupervised machine learning—learning without labeled training data—to automatically decide which parts of an application should run on near-memory processing, skipping the time-consuming step of creating labeled datasets while achieving selective offloading of only the beneficial code regions.
contributions: Unguided ML framework eliminating need for labeled training data for NMP offloading decisions
Selective offloading strategy targeting memory-intensive regions only, avoiding low-power NMP core bottleneck
1.31x performance improvement over conventional CPU-only, 1.10x over state-of-the-art offloading
16% energy savings vs. conventional, 12% vs. state-of-the-art
78% reduction in off-chip data transfer vs. conventional, 73% vs. state-of-the-art
limitations: Evaluation limited to standard benchmark suites; generalization to novel workloads unclear
Clustering approach may not capture complex application phase behavior
Does not address dynamic workload adaptation or runtime re-clustering
Limited discussion of clustering hyperparameter sensitivity
